Total Recordable Case Rate & DART Rate
Why Recordkeeping Matters

OSHA recordkeeping creates a standardized database of workplace injuries that allows: (1) companies to identify hazards and track trends, (2) OSHA to target inspections, and (3) comparison across industries using standardized incidence rates. The 200,000 basis normalizes rates for comparison regardless of company size.

The Three OSHA Forms

OSHA Form 300 — Log of Work-Related Injuries and Illnesses

The OSHA 300 Log is a running list maintained throughout the year. For each recordable case, it captures: employee name, job title, date of injury/illness, where the event occurred, description of the injury, and outcome (death, days away, restricted work, job transfer, or other recordable).

Key columns on Form 300:

  • Column G — Death
  • Column H — Days Away From Work (DAFW)
  • Column I — Job Transfer or Restriction (DJTR)
  • Column J — Other Recordable Cases
  • Columns 1–6 — Type of illness classification

Columns H + I together are used in DART Rate calculations.

OSHA Form 300A — Annual Summary

  • Summarizes the total numbers from Form 300 at year end
  • Must be certified by a company executive (owner, officer, or highest-ranking company official)
  • Must be posted in a conspicuous location accessible to employees from February 1 through April 30
  • Must be retained for 5 years following the year it covers

OSHA Form 301 — Injury and Illness Incident Report

  • Detailed incident report completed for each individual recordable case
  • Captures employee information, treating physician, treatment details, what happened and how
  • Must be completed within 7 calendar days of learning about the case
  • Equivalent first report of injury (workers' comp) form may substitute if it contains the same information
  • Retained for 5 years; confidential — employees can request access to their own Form 301

Recording Criteria — What Gets Recorded?

A case must be recorded on OSHA 300 if it is work-related AND results in:

  • Death
  • Days away from work
  • Restricted work or job transfer
  • Medical treatment beyond first aid
  • Loss of consciousness
  • Diagnosis of a significant injury/illness by a licensed health care professional

First Aid Exceptions (NOT Recordable)

The following constitute first aid and are NOT recorded on OSHA 300 (even if performed by a physician):

  • Non-prescription medication at non-prescription strength
  • Tetanus immunizations
  • Cleaning, flushing, or soaking surface wounds
  • Non-prescription wound closures (butterfly bandages, Steri-strips)
  • Non-rigid means of support (elastic bandage, non-rigid back belt)
  • Temporary immobilization as a precaution for transport
  • Drilling of fingernail to relieve pressure
  • Eye patches
  • Removing foreign bodies from eye using irrigation or cotton swab
  • Removing splinters by simple means
  • Use of finger guards
  • Use of massages

Special Recording Situations

Privacy Concern Cases

Do NOT enter the employee's name on the OSHA 300 log. Write "privacy concern case" instead. This applies to:

  • Injury/illness to an intimate body part or reproductive system
  • Sexual assault
  • Mental illness
  • HIV infection, hepatitis, or tuberculosis
  • Needle-stick injuries and cuts from contaminated sharps
  • Employee voluntarily requests privacy

Fatality Reporting (Separate from Recordkeeping)

  • Report to OSHA within 8 hours: any work-related fatality
  • Report to OSHA within 24 hours: any work-related inpatient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye
  • Report by calling 1-800-321-OSHA or local office

🧮 Mathematics — Incidence Rates

Term Final Question Context — OSHA Recordkeeping Mathematics

TF questions on this chapter typically involve: (1) filling OSHA Form 300 from a case description, (2) determining whether a case is recordable, and (3) calculating incidence rates (TRCR and DART). The Mary Louis kitchen slip case (2018-19 Q5b, 23 marks) required all three. Practice the formulas and remember the 200,000-hour basis.

The 200,000-Hour Basis — Why This Number?

200,000 hours = 100 workers × 40 hrs/week × 50 weeks/year
This represents 100 full-time equivalent (FTE) workers working a full year. By normalizing to this basis, companies of different sizes can be meaningfully compared. A company with 1,000 workers working 400,000 hours that has 10 recordable cases has the same rate as a 100-worker company with 5 cases in 200,000 hours.

Formula 1: Total Recordable Case Rate (TRCR)

TRCR = (N × 200,000) ÷ Hours Worked
N — Number of all recordable cases: deaths + days away + restricted/transfer + other recordable. Count every case that appears on the OSHA 300 log.
200,000 — The normalization constant (100 FTE workers × 40 hrs × 50 weeks). Do NOT change this number; it is a fixed standard.
Hours Worked — Actual total hours worked by ALL employees during the year (do NOT include vacation, sick leave, or holiday hours — only actual hours at work).
TRCR — Tells you: "Per 100 full-time workers, how many recordable injuries occurred this year?" Industry averages can be compared using this metric.

Formula 2: DART Rate (Days Away, Restricted, or Transferred)

DART Rate = (DART Cases × 200,000) ÷ Hours Worked
DART Cases — Only cases resulting in days away from work (Col H) OR job restriction/transfer (Col I) on OSHA 300. Does NOT include "Other Recordable Cases" (Col J) or deaths.
DART Rate — More severe than TRCR because it only counts serious cases requiring time off or job modification. Used to benchmark severity of injuries.
📌 Worked Example — Manufacturing Company Incidence Rates

Given: ABC Manufacturing has 250 employees. During the year they worked a total of 500,000 hours. They had the following OSHA 300 entries: 2 deaths, 5 cases with days away from work, 3 cases with job restriction/transfer, 4 other recordable cases.

1
Count N (total recordable cases):
N = 2 (deaths) + 5 (DAFW) + 3 (restricted/transfer) + 4 (other) = 14 cases
2
Calculate Total Recordable Case Rate (TRCR):
TRCR = (14 × 200,000) ÷ 500,000 = 2,800,000 ÷ 500,000 = 5.6
3
Count DART cases (Col H + Col I only):
DART cases = 5 (DAFW) + 3 (restricted/transfer) = 8 cases (deaths and "other" excluded)
4
Calculate DART Rate:
DART Rate = (8 × 200,000) ÷ 500,000 = 1,600,000 ÷ 500,000 = 3.2
✅ TRCR = 5.6 (meaning: 5.6 recordable injuries per 100 FTE workers) | DART Rate = 3.2 (3.2 serious cases per 100 FTE workers)
📌 Worked Example 2 — Rate Comparison Problem

Given: Company X has 50 employees who worked 100,000 hours total. They had 3 recordable cases, 2 of which involved days away from work. Company Y (competitor) has 500 employees who worked 1,000,000 hours and had 20 recordable cases, 12 with DART.

1
Company X TRCR:
(3 × 200,000) ÷ 100,000 = 6.0
2
Company Y TRCR:
(20 × 200,000) ÷ 1,000,000 = 4.0
3
Company X DART Rate:
(2 × 200,000) ÷ 100,000 = 4.0
4
Company Y DART Rate:
(12 × 200,000) ÷ 1,000,000 = 2.4
✅ Company X has a higher TRCR (6.0 vs 4.0) and higher DART Rate (4.0 vs 2.4) despite having fewer absolute cases — the 200,000-hour normalization makes the comparison fair.

Quick Review

What is the TRCR formula?
(N × 200,000) ÷ Hours Worked, where N = all recordable cases
What is the DART Rate formula?
(DART Cases × 200,000) ÷ Hours Worked, where DART = Days Away + Restricted/Transfer cases only
Why 200,000 hours?
100 workers × 40 hrs/week × 50 weeks = 200,000 hrs. It represents 100 FTE workers for a year — allows fair comparison between companies of different sizes.
What is the difference between TRCR and DART rate?
TRCR counts ALL recordable cases. DART Rate counts only cases with days away from work OR job restriction/transfer — the more serious subset.
When must Form 300A be posted?
February 1 through April 30. Must be signed by a company executive. Retained for 5 years.
What are DART cases on OSHA 300?
Cases in Column H (Days Away from Work) + Column I (Job Transfer or Restriction). Deaths and Column J "other" cases are NOT DART cases.
Name 3 first aid treatments that are NOT recordable.
Non-prescription medication, tetanus immunization, wound cleaning, butterfly bandages, eye patch, removing splinters
When is a case a "privacy concern case"?
Sexual assault, mental illness, HIV/hepatitis/TB, needle-stick injuries, intimate body part injuries. Do not enter employee's name — write "privacy concern case" on Form 300.
